1-1.text: Part one. What each digit is worth. ... Every digit sits in a place. The place tells you what the digit is worth.

1-2.text: In four thousand seven hundred and thirty five, the 7 is in the hundreds column, so it is worth 700. Four thousand seven hundred and thirty five equals 4000, plus 700, plus 30, plus 5.

1-3.text: After the decimal point come tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

1-4.text: In 3 point 4 8 2, the 8 is in the hundredths column, so it is worth 8 hundredths, which is nought point nought 8.

2-1.text: Part two. Putting numbers in order. ... To compare decimals, write them in a column with the decimal points lined up.

2-2.text: Fill the empty places with zeros, so every number has the same number of digits. A zero at the end does not change a decimal.

2-3.text: Now compare them like whole numbers: 700 is the biggest, so nought point 7 is the biggest. Nought point nought 7 is the smallest.

2-4.text: The less than sign means is less than, and the greater than sign means is greater than. The open side faces the bigger number: 3 point nought 6 is less than 3 point 6.

3-1.text: Part three. Rounding. ... Let's round 467 to the nearest 10. On a number line, 467 sits between 460 and 470.

3-2.text: 467 is closer to 470, so 467 rounded to the nearest 10 is 470.

3-3.text: The quick rule: look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to. 5 or more, round up. 4 or less, keep it the same. 3 thousand 8 hundred and 50 to the nearest 100 is 3 thousand 9 hundred.

3-4.text: Decimal places work the same way. To round 6 point 4 7 to 1 decimal place, look at the 7. It is 5 or more, so round up to 6 point 5.

4-1.text: Part four. Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000. ... When you multiply by 10, every digit moves one place to the left. 36 times 10 equals 360.

4-2.text: Times 100 moves the digits two places left. 4 point 7 times 100 equals 470. A zero fills the empty ones place.

4-3.text: Dividing moves the digits to the right. Dividing by 1000 moves them three places: 52 divided by 1000 equals nought point nought 5 2.

4-4.text: Count the zeros: 10 has one, 100 has two, 1000 has three. That is how many places the digits move.

5-1.text: Part five. Estimating. ... The first significant figure is the first digit that is not zero. To estimate, round each number to 1 significant figure.

5-2.text: 49 becomes 50, 21 becomes 20, 6 point 2 becomes 6, and nought point 3 8 becomes nought point 4.

5-3.text: Estimate 49 times 21: round to 50 times 20, which equals 1000. The exact answer is 1029, so the estimate is close.

5-4.text: Estimates help you spot mistakes. If your calculator said 102 point 9, you would know something went wrong.
